# Simulation design and performance evaluation

In this section, we present the simulation design and performance metrics for the simulation 1 and 2. The information presented here follows the suggestions from previous articles that investigated the quality of simulation studies [@siepe_etall_2024; @white_etall_2024; @morris_etall_2019].

## Simulation Conditions

Both simulations used a 2 (sample sizes) × 3 (reliability levels) × 3 (latent predictor distributions) factorial design, yielding 18 conditions. Simulation 1 evaluated UPI, LMS, QML, and LSAM; Simulation 2 excluded LMS due to computational constraints. To assess Type I error rates and empirical local power [@irmer_etall_2024], we tested two specifications: (a) linear model data generation with full model estimation (assessing Type I error), and (b) full interaction model for both generation and estimation (assessing power). This yielded 36 total conditions, each replicated 1,000 times.

Sample sizes of 400 and 1000 represented moderate to large samples. We selected 400 to examine performance below the suggested 500-threshold minimum for complex latent interaction models (Wall et al., 2012) while remaining realistic for applied research. The 1000 sample size allowed evaluation of asymptotic properties and aligned with previous simulations. Computational constraints prevented examining additional conditions. Three reliability levels (0.4, 0.6, 0.8—termed low, medium, and high) covered a broad range of measurement quality. While previous simulations typically examined high reliability [@brandt_etall_2014; @lonati_etall_2024] or contrasted high versus low [@brandt_etall_2020], we included 0.4 to assess performance under poor measurement conditions. Last, the three distributional conditions—normal, non-normal, and uniform—were based on prior research varying non-normality to different degrees [@brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @cham_etall_2012; @lonati_etall_2024; @wall_amemiya_2000].

## Data Generation

Data generation followed a similar procedure as in previous studies [@ng_chan_2020; @cox_kelcey_2021; @rosseel_etall_2025]. First, structural residual variances and measurement error variances were set to achieve $R^2 \approx 0.30$ and reliability $\rho \in \{0.4, 0.6, 0.8\}$ under normally distributed predictor latent variables. Second, using these fixed variance parameters, data were generated under three distributional conditions (see Appendix A for complete data generation procedures). See Figure 1 for the true population models. 

For Simulation 1, the dependent latent variable was generated according to:
\begin{align*}
\eta_3 = \beta_0 + \beta_1\eta_1 + \beta_2\eta_2 + \beta_3(\eta_1\eta_2) + \beta_4\eta_1^2 + \beta_5\eta_2^2 + \zeta
\end{align*}

\noindent with parameters $\beta_0 = -0.255$, $\beta_1 = \beta_2 = 0.316$, $\beta_3 = 0.139$, $\beta_4 = \beta_5 = 0.101$, and $\zeta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{33})$. For the linear model comparison, nonlinear terms were omitted ($\beta_3 = \beta_4 = \beta_5 = 0$).

For Simulation 2, the dependent latent variables followed:
\begin{align*}
\eta_4 &= \beta_{10} + \beta_{11}\eta_1 + \beta_{12}\eta_2 + \beta_{13}\eta_3 + \beta_{14}(\eta_1\eta_2) + \beta_{15}(\eta_1\eta_3) + \beta_{16}\eta_1^2 + \beta_{17}\eta_2^2 + \zeta_4 \\
\eta_5 &= \beta_{20} + \beta_{21}\eta_4 + \beta_{22}\eta_1 + \beta_{23}\eta_2 + \beta_{24}\eta_3 + \beta_{25}(\eta_1\eta_4) + \beta_{26}(\eta_2\eta_4) + \beta_{27}\eta_1^2 + \beta_{28}\eta_3^2 + \zeta_5
\end{align*}

\noindent with parameters $\beta_{10} = \beta_{20} = 0.1$, $\beta_{11} = \beta_{12} = \beta_{13} = 0.20$, $\beta_{14} = \beta_{15} = 0.11$, $\beta_{16} = \beta_{17} = 0.08$; $\beta_{21} = \beta_{22} = \beta_{23} = \beta_{24} = 0.16$, $\beta_{25} = \beta_{26} = 0.08$, $\beta_{27} = \beta_{28} = 0.06$, and $\zeta_4 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{44})$, $\zeta_5 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{55})$. For the linear model comparison, all interaction and quadratic terms were omitted.

## Reproducibility and Computational details^[All the materials to reproduce this article available on the following GitHub link: https://github.com/felipelfv/Simulation_First_PhD_Article.git. We included a `README` file that contains the step-by-step information required to reproduce the results reported, a `sessionInfo` file, the *renv* lockfile with the information for the remaining relevant packages used [@R-renv], a Dockerfile for system dependencies, and all the estimates obtained for all iterations. Moreover, this paper was written with *papaja* [@R-papaja] in Rmarkdown.]

The simulation was conducted on a Mac Studio with an Apple M4 Max chip (with 14 cores and 36 GB of RAM), running macOS Sequoia 15.5. All analyses were performed in R [@R-base] (version `r R_version`). Parallel processing was implemented through the *doParalell* package (version `r doparallel_version`) [@R-doParallel], with *doRNG* (version `r dorng_version`) [@R-doRNG] to ensure independent and reproducible random number streams. For the UPI, LMS, and QML approach, the *modsem* package was used [@kjell_etall_2024] (version `r modsem_version`). For the LSAM approach, the *lavaan* package was used [@R-lavaan] (version `r lavaan_version`). Importantly, we used the default settings for the functions provided in the packages^[This is important to acknowledge because there are arguments for the functions used that, in principle, could be tweaked to obtain better results. For instance, one could change the maximum steps for the M-step in the EM algorithm for the LMS. However, this also leads to substantial researcher degrees of freedom and hence were avoided.]. Specific to the LSAM approach, we estimated the latent factors with three different measurement blocks as opposed to a single one [@rosseel_loh_2024]. Finally, for generating normal and non-normal data we used the `rIG()` function from the *covsim* package (version `r covsim_version`) [@R-covsim] and, following the approach of @mair_etall_2012, we used the copula package for the uniform condition (version `r copula_version`) [@R-copula_b]. We acknowledge this latter procedure preserves non-normal dependencies while ensuring the exact target covariance, though the marginal distributions and copula structure are altered by the matrix transformation [@gronneberg_foldnes_2022].

## Nonconvergence and Outliers

Before analyzing the data, we inspected solutions where no estimates for the parameters of interest were produced. After ensuring these were caused by a nonconvergent estimator, we excluded the entire iteration from the analysis across estimation approaches. As noted by @lonati_etall_2024, non-convergent solutions signal replications challenging for all methods^[Convergent solutions may still be implausible or incomplete. For instance, where other estimates are not obtained. Thus, we tracked these via warnings and obtained qualitatively identical results if excluding from the analysis (results available on GitHub).]. We calculated convergence rate as $\text{Convergence}_{rate} = N_{\text{complete}}/N_{\text{total}} \times 100\%$, where $N_{\text{complete}}$ represents successfully converged replications with complete output and $N_{\text{total}}$ represents all attempted replications for the individual approach.

Following @lonati_etall_2024, we identified outliers using the box-plot method. For each method-parameter combination, estimates outside $[Q_1 - 3 \times \text{IQR}, Q_3 + 3 \times \text{IQR}]$ (where $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$) were flagged as outliers. To avoid possible arbitrary threshold selection, we also computed median estimates, median bias, and median absolute deviation (MAD) on all converged solutions before outlier removal. Thus, mean-based metrics were computed after outlier removal, whereas median-based measures were computed before (Tables 3 and 4 in the online supplementary materials contain the detailed information).

## Performance Measures

Method performance was assessed through multiple metrics following the formulas from the *simhelpers* package [@R-simhelpers], with the exception of the median-based metrics that were based on @brandt_etall_2020. The latter measures were used to complement the arbitrary decisions for deleting outliers. Following the *simhelpers* documentation and references therein, we also quantified the Monte Carlo Standard Errors (MCSE) simulation uncertainty for most of the reported performance measures using the jack-knife technique. Generally speaking, the measures are classified in terms of absolute and relative criteria measures, standard error assessment, hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals. In the main text, we only report and discuss the metrics reported in Table 1 for the interaction and quadratic effects. For the complete set of measures and main effects, we refer the reader to the online supplementary materials 1.
